data.title: Institutional concepts vs indicators: what the pros actually watch
data.description: Why most indicators are lagging reactions to what institutions have already done, and what to focus on instead.
data.author: Maono Team

institutional-concepts-vs-indicators.content:
Walk into any bank trading floor in London, New York, or Johannesburg and you will not find someone staring at a stochastic oscillator, waiting for the RSI to cross 30, or counting Bollinger Band touches.

What you will find is people watching price, structure, and flow. They are reading where liquidity is sitting, where large orders need to be filled, and how price is reacting around those zones.

This is not a gatekeeping argument. Indicators have their place. But retail traders tend to get stuck on them, and it helps to understand why.

## What an indicator actually is

Every indicator you have ever seen is a mathematical transformation of price. It takes the last N candles, runs a formula, and plots the result.

That means every indicator is, by definition, **lagging**. It describes what already happened. A 20-period moving average tells you the average of the last 20 closes. A MACD crossover tells you two moving averages have crossed. None of it predicts anything. It describes.

This is fine as context. It is a problem when it is used as a trigger.

## What institutions are watching instead

Professional traders care about a short list of things, and price action is the common thread:

- **Market structure.** Higher highs and higher lows, or lower highs and lower lows. Is the trend intact? Has it broken?
- **Liquidity.** Where are stop losses clustered? Where would a smart seller find enough buyers to unload a large position?
- **Order blocks and imbalance.** The candles where price moved aggressively. Those zones often get retested before price continues.
- **Session behaviour.** London open, New York open, the overlap, the Asian range. Each session has a personality.

None of this requires a new indicator. It requires understanding how money moves.

## Why retail traders fight this

The honest answer is that institutional concepts are harder to teach and harder to monetise. It is easier to sell a course that says "buy when RSI is oversold" than to sit with a student for an hour and work through why a 4-hour swing high is meaningful.

YouTube and social media optimise for simple. The market does not.

## A worked example

Take any major pair during London open. Mark the previous day's high and low. Mark the Asian range high and low. Mark the weekly high and low.

Now watch what happens when price approaches those levels. You will see rejections, retests, and breakouts with follow-through. You will also see a lot of noise. The skill is in telling those apart.

No indicator will do that for you. A consistent framework will.

## Where to start

If you have been trading indicators and feeling like you are always a candle late, that feeling is not in your head. You are trading a lagging signal.

The shift to institutional concepts takes time. It is not a new shortcut. It is the long way around that actually leads somewhere.

Start with one idea: learn to mark structure on one pair, on one timeframe, for one month. That alone will teach you more than any new oscillator.

data.title: Trading psychology: the case for a daily journal
data.description: Why the traders who journal outperform the ones who do not, and what to actually write in it.
data.author: Maono Team

journaling-for-consistency.content:
The gap between a mediocre trader and a consistent one is rarely about strategy. It is about self-awareness.

A trading journal is the cheapest tool available for closing that gap. It costs nothing. It takes ten minutes a day. It is also the habit most traders refuse to keep, which is probably why most traders stay where they are.

## What a journal is not

A journal is not a spreadsheet of trades with a PnL column. That is a track record. Useful, but different.

A journal is a written record of **what you thought, what you did, and why**. The PnL is the smallest part of it. The reasoning is the whole point.

## What to write

Before the trade:

- What is the setup I am seeing?
- What is my entry, stop, and target?
- What is the size of my risk in currency terms?
- How do I feel right now? Calm, anxious, desperate to trade?

After the trade:

- Did I follow my plan?
- If I broke a rule, which one and why?
- What was happening in my head during the trade?
- What is one sentence of honest feedback to myself?

The pre-trade section catches impulsive trades. Forcing yourself to write the reason slows you down enough that half of your worst trades will not get taken.

The post-trade section catches patterns. Over a month, you will see that you break the same rule in the same emotional state. That is actionable. You cannot fix a problem you have not named.

## The weekly review

On Sunday, read through the week's entries. Look for patterns, not outcomes.

Questions to ask:

- Which trades this week did I take outside my plan?
- What emotion was I feeling when I took them?
- Were my winning trades my best trades, or lucky ones?
- Were my losing trades mistakes, or just normal variance?

The distinction between a bad trade and a bad outcome is everything. A trade that followed the plan and lost is fine. A trade that broke the plan and won is dangerous, because it teaches you the wrong lesson.

## Why it works

Writing slows you down. That is the mechanism. Trading is mostly a speed game where your brain wants to act faster than your discipline allows. Journaling introduces friction at the exact moment you need it.

Over time, the journal becomes a mirror. You see who you actually are as a trader, not who you imagined you were. That is uncomfortable, which is why most traders stop after two weeks.

The ones who do not stop are the ones who end up consistent.

## Start smaller than you think

Do not design a perfect journal template. Do not buy software. Open a Google Doc and write one paragraph about every trade you take this week. That is enough to start.

If you cannot commit ten minutes a day to understanding how you trade, the honest conclusion is that trading is not for you yet. That is okay. The journal will tell you that too.

And that is worth more than the next indicator.

data.title: The 1% risk rule, explained without the math
data.description: Why professional traders risk so little per trade, and how the rule actually protects you from yourself.
data.author: Maono Team

one-percent-risk-rule.content:
The most boring rule in trading is also the one that keeps accounts alive: never risk more than 1 percent of your account on a single trade.

Most new traders hear this, nod, and then promptly ignore it. It sounds too slow. "I need to grow my account. 1 percent is nothing."

That reaction is exactly why most new accounts do not survive the first year.

## What 1 percent actually means

On a R10,000 account, 1 percent is R100. That is your maximum loss on a trade. If the trade goes against you, you lose R100 and you move on.

The 1 percent is not the size of the position. It is the size of the loss if your stop gets hit. A R100 risk with a 50-pip stop means a completely different position size than a R100 risk with a 10-pip stop. Most trading platforms have a position size calculator for exactly this reason.

## Why the rule exists

The rule is not about being cautious. It is about being **unkillable**.

If you risk 1 percent per trade, ten losses in a row puts you down roughly 9.5 percent. Uncomfortable, but survivable. You can recover.

If you risk 5 percent per trade, ten losses in a row puts you down 40 percent. You now need a 67 percent return just to get back to even. Your judgement is compromised. Your confidence is shot. You are the trader who starts revenge trading.

**Professional traders do not risk small because they are timid. They risk small because they know variance is real, and even a great strategy has losing streaks.**

## The hidden benefit

There is a psychological benefit to the rule that no one talks about.

When 1 percent is at risk, you can be wrong without panicking. You can let the trade play out. You can follow your plan. You do not move your stop loss. You do not close early in fear.

The trader who risks 5 percent is managing an emotion. The trader who risks 1 percent is managing a process.

## What to do with this

If you are currently risking more than 1 percent per trade, the fix is immediate: calculate 1 percent of your account, calculate your stop distance, and use a lot size that matches. That is it.

You will not get rich faster by risking more. You will just get stopped out earlier.

The point of trading is not to win the next trade. It is to still be trading in five years. The 1 percent rule is how you get there.

data.title: How to build a trading plan you will actually follow
data.description: A short, honest framework for a trading plan that survives contact with a bad Monday morning.
data.author: Maono Team

trading-plan-you-will-follow.content:
Every trading book tells you to write a trading plan. Most traders write a two-page document, read it once, and never look at it again.

The problem is not that traders are lazy. The problem is that most plans are written for a version of the trader that does not exist, the one who reads their plan before every trade and follows it calmly at 03:00 during a news spike.

This is a shorter, more honest framework. A plan that fits on one page and survives contact with a bad Monday morning.

## Part one: when you trade

Before you think about setups, answer three questions:

- What sessions will you trade? London, New York, the overlap, or the Asian range?
- What days will you trade? Some traders skip Mondays and Fridays because of the weekend gap and Friday volatility.
- What news events make you stand aside? NFP, CPI, central bank rate decisions are the usual list.

Decide this once. Write it down. Stick to it. Most undisciplined trades come from trading outside the hours you perform best in.

## Part two: what you trade

Pick your pairs. Most traders would be better off specialising in two or three pairs than skimming through twelve. You learn the personality of a pair by trading it, not by reading about it.

Decide on your timeframes. A clean setup needs a higher timeframe (4H or daily) for context and a lower timeframe (15m or 1H) for entry. If you are always flipping between 1m, 5m, and 4H, you are not executing, you are searching.

## Part three: the setup, in plain language

Write your A+ setup in a single paragraph that a friend could read and understand.

Something like: *"I take a trade when price breaks a higher timeframe level with momentum, retraces into the prior structure, and shows rejection on the 15-minute. I enter on the first valid candle close, stop goes above the recent swing, target is the next major level."*

That is a plan. Not a flowchart. Not a 50-page PDF. A paragraph.

If you cannot write your setup in one paragraph, you do not have a setup. You have a vibe.

## Part four: risk and management

Three numbers. Write them down.

1. Max risk per trade, as a percentage (1 percent or less).
2. Max open risk at any one time (usually 2 to 3 percent across all trades).
3. Daily loss limit that ends your session (often 2 to 3 percent).

When the daily limit is hit, you stop. Close the platform. The point is not punishment. The point is that after two losses in a row, your judgement is already worse than it was an hour ago. Stopping protects tomorrow.

## Part five: the review

Every Sunday, take ten minutes:

- Did I follow my plan this week?
- Which trades broke the rules?
- What was the emotional state behind those trades?
- What is one thing to change next week?

The review is the plan. Writing a plan and not reviewing it is like making a budget and never checking your bank account.

## Keep it one page

Your entire plan should fit on one printed page. If it is longer, it is a manual, and no one reads the manual.

The goal is not to write a beautiful plan. The goal is to build a set of rules you are actually willing to follow at 07:00 on a Monday after a losing week.

Start short. Iterate.

data.title: Why most retail traders lose (and how to flip the odds)
data.description: The three reasons most retail traders blow their accounts, and how a process-first approach changes the outcome.
data.author: Maono Team

why-retail-traders-lose.content:
Open any forex statistic and the same number comes up: roughly 70 to 90 percent of retail traders lose money over a twelve-month period. That number is not a coincidence, and it is not bad luck. It is the predictable result of how retail traders approach the market.

If you are on the wrong side of that statistic, the good news is that the fix is not a secret indicator or a smarter strategy. The fix is a process.

## Reason one: over-leverage

Most new traders do not start with a blown account because their analysis was wrong. They blow up because a single trade was too big to survive.

The math is simple. If you risk 20 percent of your account on one trade and you are wrong twice in a row, you are down roughly 36 percent. You now need a 56 percent recovery just to get back to even. That is before you have even started making money.

Professional desks do not trade this way. They risk a fraction of a percent per idea, so that being wrong five times in a row is inconvenient, not fatal.

## Reason two: strategy hopping

The second killer is switching systems after every losing streak. A trader tries a moving average crossover, loses four times, reads about supply and demand on YouTube, switches, loses three more times, switches again.

The problem is not the strategy. The problem is that no approach has been given a long enough run to produce a statistically meaningful sample. You cannot judge an edge from ten trades. You need fifty, preferably a hundred.

**The fix is to pick one methodology and commit to it for at least one full quarter of consistent application** before you allow yourself to evaluate whether it works.

## Reason three: no journal, no review

If a trader cannot tell you why their last five trades worked and why the next five did not, they are not trading. They are gambling with charts.

A trading journal does three things:

- Forces you to articulate your setup before you take it, which catches most impulsive trades.
- Creates a record you can actually review, so patterns become visible.
- Turns emotional losses into data, which is easier to look at on a Sunday afternoon than in the moment.

You do not need software for this. A Google Sheet is fine. What matters is that every trade has a written reason, a planned risk, and a post-trade note.

## How to flip the odds

The traders who survive the first year share three habits, and none of them are about finding a better entry signal:

1. They risk a fixed, small percentage per trade, usually one percent or less.
2. They trade one methodology long enough to gather real evidence on it.
3. They journal every trade and review the journal weekly.

None of that is exciting. It does not make for a good social media post. But it is the actual difference between the 10 percent who last and the 90 percent who do not.

The market does not pay for being clever. It pays for being consistent.

data.title: EURUSD weekly breakdown: what we're watching
data.description: How we read EURUSD into a new trading week, using structure, key levels, and session behaviour.

eurusd-weekly-breakdown.content:
This is an example of how we prepare for a trading week inside the community. No live signals, no predictions — just the process we go through on a Sunday evening before Monday opens.

## Step 1: Context on the weekly

First question: **is price in trend, or in range, on the weekly chart?**

On EURUSD right now, we are in a multi-month range between roughly 1.0600 and 1.1100. That matters because range behaviour is different from trend behaviour. In a range, the edges are where the trades are. In a trend, pullbacks are where the trades are.

If you do not know which mode the market is in, you will fight the wrong battle all week.

## Step 2: Mark the levels on the daily

Three levels we care about this week:

- **1.0850** — mid-range, reacted four times in the last six weeks. Decision point.
- **1.0940** — previous week's high, and a 4-hour supply zone.
- **1.0760** — previous month's low and a clean demand zone.

That is it. Three levels, three reasons. Anything else is noise until price gets near one of them.

## Step 3: Plan the reactions, not the direction

We do not predict where EURUSD will go this week. We plan what we will do **if** it reaches a level.

- If price pushes into 1.0940 and shows rejection on the 4-hour, we are looking for shorts back toward 1.0850.
- If price breaks 1.0940 with momentum and retests it cleanly, we flip long, targeting 1.1020.
- If price breaks 1.0760 to the downside, we stand aside and wait for the next level, because the range is invalidated and we do not yet know what the new context is.

## Step 4: Know when not to trade

Big data events this week: CPI on Wednesday, ECB on Thursday. Our default around those is to close open trades thirty minutes before release and not re-enter for at least an hour after. News days create unreliable reactions at levels. That is not where our edge is.

## Why we share this

The point of a weekly breakdown is not to be right about direction. It is to get to Friday with a clean set of notes about what actually happened versus what we expected, so the Sunday review the next week is meaningful.

Over a year, the pattern in your notes is your edge. Before you can study the pattern, you have to keep the notes.

## Try it this week

Pick one pair. Spend twenty minutes on Sunday evening doing steps one to four above. On Friday night, review. Even if you never take a trade, you will understand the pair better than 90% of retail traders do.

data.title: Position sizing, explained with a calculator
data.description: The simple formula that turns any stop loss into a correctly-sized trade, with worked examples in rands.

position-size-calculator.content:
Position sizing is the most important skill in trading, and the one most people never learn properly.

Here is the whole concept on one page, with numbers you can actually use.

## The goal

Every trade should risk the **same amount of money**, regardless of the stop loss size. If you risk R100 per trade, you risk R100 whether your stop is 5 pips away or 50.

The lot size changes. The risk does not.

## The formula

Risk amount = Account balance × Risk percentage

Lot size = Risk amount ÷ (Stop loss in pips × Pip value)

That is it. Three numbers. Every trading platform has a built-in calculator for the second line, so you do not have to memorise pip values for every pair.

## Worked example

Let us say:

- Account: R20,000
- Risk per trade: 1% → R200
- Stop loss: 30 pips
- Pair: EURUSD, standard account

For EURUSD, one standard lot moves by R170 per pip (roughly, depending on exchange rate).

Position size = R200 ÷ (30 × R170) = 0.039 lots, so about 0.04 standard lots, or 0.4 mini lots.

If you punch this into your broker, the trade will lose exactly R204 if it hits the stop. That is the number you wanted.

## Why this matters more than your strategy

Two traders use the same strategy. Both win 55% of trades with a 1:1.5 risk-to-reward.

Trader A risks 1% per trade. After 100 trades, account is up about 20%. Reasonable.

Trader B eyeballs position size and sometimes risks 1%, sometimes 3%, sometimes 5% when they are feeling confident. After 100 trades, account is down 12%. Same strategy. Different outcome.

The strategy did not fail. The sizing failed.

## Three rules

- **Decide your risk percent before opening the chart.** Not after seeing the setup.
- **Never size up a position because you are "really sure."** Confidence is not a risk parameter.
- **If you cannot enter the trade at the correct size, skip it.** Do not reduce the stop to fit a bigger position. The stop is defined by the structure, not by your account.

## Try it

Calculate your next three trades using the formula above. Write down the risk amount beforehand. Compare it to what you actually lost when a trade stopped out.

If the two numbers match, your sizing works. If they do not, your sizing is broken and it does not matter what your strategy is.

data.title: How to read a candlestick properly
data.description: A short, practical guide to what a candle is actually telling you — beyond open, high, low, close.

reading-candlesticks.content:
Most new traders learn the four prices on a candle and stop there. A candle is more useful than that. It is a story about who was in control during that window of time.

## The four prices, quickly

Every candle shows:

- **Open** — where price started
- **High** — the highest it reached
- **Low** — the lowest it reached
- **Close** — where it finished

Bullish candles close above their open. Bearish candles close below. This is the easy part.

## What the body is saying

The **body** is the distance between open and close. It tells you how decisive the move was.

- **Large body, small wicks** — one side dominated the entire window. Strong intent.
- **Small body, long wicks** — both sides fought, and nobody closed the deal. Indecision.
- **Small body near a level** — often a better signal than a big body, especially at a key support or resistance.

A huge green candle is not always bullish. If it closes into a major resistance, it often marks the point where sellers step in.

## What the wicks are saying

Wicks are rejections. They show where price went but could not stay.

- A long upper wick means price pushed up, then got sold back down. Supply stepped in.
- A long lower wick means price pushed down, then got bought back up. Demand stepped in.

Wicks at key levels are one of the clearest signals of institutional participation. If a 4-hour candle prints a long lower wick into a daily support, that is not noise — that is someone buying.

## Context is everything

A bullish engulfing candle in the middle of a range is worth nothing. The same candle at the bottom of a swing, into a level you had already marked, is a potential trade.

Never read a candle in isolation. Always ask:

- Where is price in the bigger picture?
- What level is this candle forming at?
- What has the last three candles been doing?

The candle is the trigger. The level is the reason.

## Where to take this next

If you find candlesticks interesting, **support, resistance, and structure** is the next piece. Candles at random points on the chart are just shapes. Candles at levels are setups.

Join the free signals group — every post shows candles in context, so you get used to reading them the way institutions do.

data.title: Support and resistance: a one-page cheatsheet
data.description: How to mark levels that actually matter, and ignore the ones that don't.

support-and-resistance-cheatsheet.content:
Support and resistance is the most misused concept in trading. Most charts you see online have a level drawn on every second swing. That is not support and resistance. That is clutter.

Here is a one-page version of how to do it properly.

## Start from the top down

Always start on the **higher timeframe**. Daily first. Then 4-hour. Only then look at the 1-hour.

On the daily, mark no more than five levels on any pair. If you have more than five, you are marking noise.

## What makes a level real

A valid level has three things:

- **Multiple touches** — price has respected it more than once.
- **A clean reaction** — the reaction was fast and directional, not sideways chop.
- **Recency** — it has mattered in the last three to six months. A 2019 level on EURUSD is not your concern.

If a level does not have all three, skip it.

## Draw with zones, not lines

Levels are not pixels wide. Draw a zone — the wick on one side, the body close on the other. Price reacts inside the zone, not exactly on a line.

A zone that is too wide is useless. Keep it to the extremes of the meaningful candles in the area.

## Ignore these "levels"

- **Micro levels on the 5-minute** — they exist, but they are not tradable on their own.
- **Round numbers** for the sake of round numbers — 1.1000 only matters if price has reacted there.
- **Fibonacci retracement levels** — useful as context, not as "levels" in the support/resistance sense.
- **Trendlines drawn from two points** — one more touch does not make a trendline. You need at least three.

## What to do when price reaches a level

Do not trade the level. Trade the **reaction** at the level.

A clean pin bar or engulfing candle rejecting a daily support is a signal. A break and retest of a 4-hour resistance is a signal. Price simply arriving at a level is not.

## Weekly ritual

Every Sunday, re-mark your charts on the daily and 4-hour. If your levels from last week still hold up, keep them. If they were invalidated, delete them and draw new ones.

Your chart should get cleaner over time, not busier.

## Next step

Join the free signals group — every daily idea we share starts with a level. Over a few weeks you will see the pattern: clean levels, clean setups.

data.title: A no-nonsense forex glossary
data.description: The 30 terms you actually need to know, explained in plain English.

trading-glossary.content:
Most trading glossaries are copy-pasted from textbooks. This one is the thirty terms we use every day inside the community, explained the way we would explain them to a new member.

## The basics

- **Pip** — the smallest standard price movement. On EURUSD, a pip is the fourth decimal. 1.1000 → 1.1001 is one pip.
- **Lot** — the unit of a position. One standard lot is 100,000 units of the base currency. Mini lot is 10,000. Micro lot is 1,000.
- **Leverage** — how much bigger your position is than your account. 1:100 leverage means R1,000 in your account controls R100,000 of currency. Amplifies both wins and losses.
- **Spread** — the gap between buy and sell price. This is what your broker charges you on every trade.
- **Long** — a buy position. You profit if price goes up.
- **Short** — a sell position. You profit if price goes down.

## Charting

- **Candlestick** — a single price window showing open, high, low, and close.
- **Timeframe** — how much time one candle represents. M5 = five minutes. H1 = one hour. D1 = one day.
- **Higher timeframe (HTF)** — daily and up. Used for context.
- **Lower timeframe (LTF)** — 1-hour and below. Used for entries.
- **Structure** — the pattern of highs and lows on a chart. Higher highs and higher lows = uptrend. Lower highs and lower lows = downtrend.

## Levels

- **Support** — a zone where price has historically stopped falling.
- **Resistance** — a zone where price has historically stopped rising.
- **Supply zone** — a wider version of resistance, showing where sellers previously dominated.
- **Demand zone** — a wider version of support, showing where buyers previously dominated.
- **Liquidity** — a cluster of stop losses or pending orders. Institutional traders hunt these.

## Trade mechanics

- **Stop loss** — the price at which you accept the trade is wrong and close it.
- **Take profit** — the price at which you accept the trade worked and close it.
- **Risk-to-reward (RR)** — the ratio of what you stand to lose vs. what you stand to make. 1:2 means risking R100 to make R200.
- **Breakeven** — moving your stop to your entry price, so the trade cannot lose.

## Psychology

- **Overtrading** — taking trades that do not meet your plan. Usually driven by revenge, boredom, or FOMO.
- **FOMO** — fear of missing out. The feeling that makes you chase price without a setup.
- **Revenge trading** — trying to immediately win back what you just lost. Almost always makes it worse.
- **Tilt** — being in an emotional state where your decisions no longer follow your plan.
- **Discipline** — the only real edge. Everything else is technique.

## Market types

- **Trend** — price moving consistently in one direction, with higher highs and higher lows, or the inverse.
- **Range** — price oscillating between two horizontal levels, with no clear directional bias.
- **Breakout** — price moving decisively beyond a level it had previously respected.
- **Retest** — price returning to a broken level to confirm it as new support or resistance.

## News and sessions

- **Session** — the period when a particular financial centre is most active. London, New York, and Tokyo are the main three.
- **NFP** — Non-Farm Payrolls. US jobs data released on the first Friday of each month. Usually volatile.
- **CPI** — Consumer Price Index. Inflation data. Major market mover.
- **Rate decision** — when a central bank announces whether it is raising, holding, or lowering interest rates.

## One more thing

Do not try to memorise this list. Use it as a lookup. Every week you will come across one or two terms you were not sure about. Come back here. Over a few months, they all become second nature.

If a term we use inside the community is not on this list and you want it explained, WhatsApp us. We will add it.

what-is-forex-trading.content:
## The forex market in plain English

Forex (foreign exchange) is the global marketplace where currencies are bought and sold. It is the largest financial market in the world, over $7 trillion trades hands every single day.

Unlike stock markets, forex has no central exchange. It operates 24 hours a day, five days a week, across major financial centres in Sydney, Tokyo, London, and New York.

## Who trades forex?

- **Central banks**, Setting monetary policy, defending currency pegs, managing reserves
- **Commercial banks**, Facilitating international trade and corporate hedging
- **Hedge funds and institutional traders**, Speculation, arbitrage, and macro positioning
- **Retail traders**, Individuals like you, trading through brokers

## Why do most retail traders lose?

Retail traders represent a tiny fraction of daily volume. When you place a buy order, you are trading against banks, funds, and algorithms with far more information, capital, and infrastructure than you have.

Most retail strategies, based on lagging indicators like RSI, MACD, and moving averages, generate signals after institutions have already moved price.

## The institutional edge

Understanding how institutions think, where they place orders, how they create liquidity traps, how they engineer price to fill large positions, is the edge that separates consistent traders from guessers.

This is what we teach at Maono.

## Ready to learn more?

Join the free signals group to see how we analyse markets, then explore our structured course curriculum when you are ready to go deeper.
